source: Kahneman and Lovallo (1993) Timid choices and bold forecasts: a cognitive perspective on risk taking. Management Science 39(1):17-31
finding: Founding statement of inside versus outside view. Inside view: focus on the case, its plan and obstacles, build scenarios, extrapolate trends. Outside view: ignore case details, use the statistics of a class of similar cases, then place the case in that distribution. The authors say the outside view is much more likely to be realistic when both are applied with equal skill.
numbers: No experiment here. Theory paper with a worked story and a literature review.
quote: The outside view ... essentially ignores the details of the case at hand, and involves no attempt at detailed forecasting of the future history of the project.
limits: Theory paper. The outside view is conservative: it fails on extreme and exceptional events and does well on common ones. It needs a class that can be defined.
agent_relevance: This is the S0 gate in plain form: before building a plan or scenario, ask what happened in similar cases and where this case sits in that distribution.

source: Kahneman and Lovallo (1993) Timid choices and bold forecasts: a cognitive perspective on risk taking. Management Science 39(1):17-31
finding: The curriculum story (Israel, 1976). A team of academics and teachers estimated time to a complete draft. Every estimate, including Kahneman's, fell between 18 and 30 months. The curriculum expert, asked for similar past teams, said about 40% never finished, and none of the rest took under 7 years or over 10. He saw no factor that favoured the team and thought they were slightly below average. The team ignored the forecast. The project finished about 8 years later.
numbers: Inside estimates 18-30 months. Outside class: about 40% abandoned, 7-10 years for the rest. Actual: about 8 years. N=1 team; the expert recalled the class from memory.
quote: About 40% of them eventually gave up. Of the remaining, I cannot think of any that was completed in less than seven years
limits: Anecdote, not a controlled test. The class was recalled from one expert's memory, not counted from data. The team's agreement did not make the forecast valid.
agent_relevance: A class can be built by asking 'how long did similar attempts take, and how many never finished?' Failure rate is part of the base rate. Also: agreement among inside-view forecasters is not evidence.

source: Kahneman and Lovallo (1993) Timid choices and bold forecasts: a cognitive perspective on risk taking. Management Science 39(1):17-31
finding: Three further features of the story. Consensus is not validity, because a shared flaw in reasoning produces consensus. Statistical knowledge a person holds is not retrieved when they forecast by the inside view (the expert's first estimate matched the others). Facing the outside-view facts was demoralising, so the forecast was quietly dropped.
numbers: No numbers. Cites base-rate studies where stated personal information gets weight but known statistics are largely ignored.
limits: Mechanism claims, supported by the cited literature rather than by a test inside this paper.
agent_relevance: The scaffold must force the base-rate lookup as a code-driven step. The model will not retrieve it on its own, and an unwelcome base rate must not be dropped.

source: Kahneman and Lovallo (1993) Timid choices and bold forecasts: a cognitive perspective on risk taking. Management Science 39(1):17-31
finding: Entrepreneur example (Cooper et al. 1988, quoted). New entrepreneurs gave their own chance of success and also the success rate for businesses like theirs. Their own chances were uncorrelated with objective predictors such as education, supervisory experience and starting capital. The class estimate was much closer to the truth than the own-venture estimate.
numbers: Over 80% rated own chance of success at 70% or better. One third said success was certain. Mean chance given for a business like theirs: 59%. Real five-year survival of new firms: about 33% (Dun and Bradstreet 1967).
limits: Second-hand report of Cooper et al. Even the class estimate (59%) was optimistic. The inside view is not always optimistic: worried parents of rebellious teens are too pessimistic.
agent_relevance: Shows the split inside the same head: the person knows the class rate but does not apply it to their own case. A scaffold can ask for both numbers and show the gap.

source: Kahneman and Lovallo (1993) Timid choices and bold forecasts: a cognitive perspective on risk taking. Management Science 39(1):17-31
finding: Evidence that planned projects run late and over budget. Rand study of pioneer process plants: almost all construction costs exceeded estimates by over 20%, and the norm was more than double. PIMS data on start-up ventures: over 80% fell short of planned market share. The authors also explain why optimism wins organisational contests: winner's curse and regression to the mean (the project forecast to be best is the one most likely to fall short).
numbers: Over 20% overrun in almost all pioneer plants; costs more than doubled as the norm (Merrow et al. 1981). Over 80% below planned market share (PIMS, via Davis 1985).
limits: Cited from earlier studies, not re-checked. Applies most when the project is new technology or unfamiliar ground.
agent_relevance: Selection effect: the plan that survives a competition is biased upward. A scaffold that picks its best-looking candidate should expect that candidate's claimed quality to shrink.

source: Kahneman and Lovallo (1993) Timid choices and bold forecasts: a cognitive perspective on risk taking. Management Science 39(1):17-31
finding: Advice on choosing the class. The class is ambiguous in many cases (the firm's own past ventures or the most similar developments elsewhere). The authors advise trying both and choosing units that allow comparison, such as actual divided by planned spending. They also name a real dilemma: realism has costs, since optimism may raise persistence and morale.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Offers no rule for resolving two classes that disagree. Calls the realism versus morale tension a genuine dilemma with no simple rule.
agent_relevance: Run more than one comparison class and report the spread. Disagreement between classes is itself a signal of uncertainty to carry into the answer.

source: Kahneman and Lovallo (1993) Timid choices and bold forecasts: a cognitive perspective on risk taking. Management Science 39(1):17-31
finding: Link to base-rate research. The paper says that when only personal information is offered, relevant statistics the person already knows are largely ignored (Kahneman and Tversky 1973; Tversky and Kahneman 1983), and that explicitly stated statistics have some effect but less than they should (Griffin and Tversky 1992; Lynch and Ofir 1989). It also notes a calibration oddity: item-by-item overconfidence (about 80% correct when '99% sure') but accurate or slightly pessimistic global estimates of total hits.
numbers: About 80% correct when 99% sure. No overconfidence in after-session estimates of the number of questions answered correctly (Gigerenzer et al. 1991; Griffin and Tversky 1992).
limits: Cited findings, not reproduced in this paper. The global-versus-item calibration gap is contested in the overconfidence literature.
agent_relevance: A class-level question ('how many of these will I get right?') may give better-calibrated numbers than item-level confidence. Candidate for a code-run step: ask for the count, then spread it across items.

source: Flyvbjerg (2006) From Nobel Prize to project management: getting risks right. Project Management Journal 37(3):5-15
finding: Defines reference class forecasting (RCF) as a three-step method: (1) pick a reference class of comparable past projects, (2) get the distribution of outcomes for that class, (3) place the specific project in that distribution. It forecasts by regressing the best guess toward the class mean and widening the interval toward the class interval. It does not try to predict specific events for the project.
numbers: Three steps. Cites Kahneman and Tversky (1979b, p. 326) for the regression-to-class-mean framing.
limits: Review by an advocate. Step 1 (class choice) is left to judgment.
agent_relevance: A direct recipe for S0: class, distribution, position. The agent can output a distribution and a percentile, not only a point.

source: Flyvbjerg (2006) From Nobel Prize to project management
finding: Cost overrun and demand data for transport projects: forecasts are biased, not just noisy. Average cost overrun in constant prices was 44.7% for rail, 33.8% for bridges and tunnels, 20.4% for roads. Rail passenger forecasts were wrong on average by 51.4% (too high). No improvement in accuracy over the 70-year cost record or the 30-year demand record.
numbers: Cost: rail 44.7% (sd 38.4, p<0.001), bridges and tunnels 33.8%, roads 20.4% (p=0.004 as read). Traffic: rail -51.4% (sd 28.1); 84% of rail forecasts off by more than 20%; roads +9.5% (sd 44.3), half off by more than 20%. Table 1 layout is garbled in the extracted text, so the sd and p values per type are uncertain.
limits: Database of large transport projects; not a random sample of all projects. Flyvbjerg argues the pattern fits political pressure better than technical error or psychology.
agent_relevance: Class data show a direction as well as a size of error. A correction can be applied by code: shift the inside estimate by the class bias.

source: Flyvbjerg (2006) From Nobel Prize to project management
finding: First practical RCF: UK Department for Transport optimism-bias uplifts, built from reference classes. For roads a class of 172 completed projects gave the distribution of overruns; the uplift depends on how much overrun risk the owner accepts.
numbers: Roads: 40% of projects overran by at most 10%, 80% by at most 32%. Uplift on budget: roads 15% at the 50th percentile and 32% at the 80th; rail 40% and 57%; fixed links 23% and 55%. Building projects 4-51%; IT projects 10-200%. First live use: Edinburgh tram, Oct 2004.
limits: Uplifts are descriptive of the past class. Wide ranges for IT and buildings show the class is heterogeneous. Edinburgh tram use is a case, not a controlled test.
agent_relevance: Percentile choice is a risk-appetite dial. The agent can state its answer at a chosen percentile of the class instead of a single number.

source: Flyvbjerg (2006) From Nobel Prize to project management (reporting Lovallo and Kahneman 2003)
finding: A short outside-view prompt reduced optimism in a student study. A group of incoming students rated their future performance and expected to beat 84% of peers, which cannot be true for all. A second group first answered questions about entrance scores and peers' scores, then rated themselves; their average rating fell by 20%, though still overconfident.
numbers: 84% expected to beat peers. 20% lower expected-performance rating after the outside-view questions. Group sizes not given in this source.
limits: Second-hand through Flyvbjerg citing Lovallo and Kahneman (2003, p. 61) citing Gilovich et al. (2002). Original N unknown to us. Treat as a single reported result.
agent_relevance: A cheap diversion to class facts before the self-estimate moves the estimate. Suggests an order rule: class facts first, case details second.

source: Flyvbjerg, Hon and Fok (2016) Reference class forecasting for Hong Kong's major roadworks projects. Proc. ICE Civil Eng. 169(6):17-24
finding: Hong Kong test of RCF: 25 roadworks projects (1993-2011) compared against an Oxford benchmark of 863 road projects from 34 countries. Estimates made later in the project (closer to construction) were more accurate, and by the last estimate stage the median was about unbiased.
numbers: Cost overrun: benchmark +20%, HK +11% at decision to build (Cat C), +6% (Cat B), -1% (Cat A). Share of projects overrunning: benchmark 9 in 10, HK 7 in 10 at Cat C (p=0.006), 5 in 10 at Cat A. Schedule overrun: benchmark +38%, HK +58% (p=0.089, not significant); 8 in 10 late in HK vs 6 in 10 (p=0.048). Mean duration 8.9 vs 5.5 years (p<0.001). HK class uplifts: +13% at a 50% accepted overrun risk, +44% at a low accepted risk (as read).
limits: Small local sample (23, 22 and 20 usable projects per stage). Only the Cat C stage is comparable to the benchmark. The cost difference from benchmark is not significant. This study measured the class; it did not test whether using it improved later decisions.
agent_relevance: A local class can differ from the global one (here: cheaper on cost, worse on time). Report which class was used and check local data when it exists.

source: Flyvbjerg and Sunstein (2016) The principle of the malevolent hiding hand; or, the planning fallacy writ large. Social Research 83(4)
finding: Test of Hirschman's Hiding Hand (benefit overruns tend to beat cost overruns) on a large project sample. Cost overruns generally beat benefit overruns, which supports the planning fallacy over the Hiding Hand as the typical pattern. Only about one in five projects showed the benevolent pattern.
numbers: Sample of 2,062 projects with cost data; 327 with both cost and benefit data. Benefit overrun larger than cost overrun in 22% of those 327 (78% not), p<0.0001; by type: dams 18%, rail 17%, tunnels 21%, power plants 26%, buildings 28%, bridges 38% (p=0.22, not significant), roads 25%. Cost ratio actual/estimate all types about 1.39-1.43 vs benefit ratio about 0.83-0.9.
limits: Authors are proponents of the planning fallacy view. Sample of large public projects, not all ventures. Bridges are the one type where the result is not significant.
agent_relevance: Boundary: in about a fifth of cases the class bias runs the other way. The class base rate is a prior, not a guarantee. Keep the tail.

source: Flyvbjerg (2018) Planning fallacy or hiding hand: which is the better explanation? World Development 103:383-386
finding: Reply to critics. Agrees the Hiding Hand exists but shows it occurs in one fifth of projects, so it is not typical. Notes the two theories differ on benefits: Hiding Hand predicts both costs and benefits underestimated, optimism bias predicts costs underestimated and benefits overestimated. Also criticises Hirschman's original sample (11 projects, sampled on the outcome).
numbers: 80% of projects not showing Hiding Hand behaviour. Hirschman's original sample: 11 projects.
limits: Single-author rejoinder in a debate. The critics' own data (a survey of World Bank supervisors) are disputed; we did not read them.
agent_relevance: Competing explanation to hold in view: some inside-view surprises are positive. The outside view should give a two-sided distribution.

source: Flyvbjerg (2003) Delusions of success: comment on Lovallo and Kahneman. HBR December, pp. 121-122
finding: Main challenge to the psychological explanation. Forecasters made the same size of error for 70 years, and specialist forecasters called in from outside should learn. Flyvbjerg's tests of technical, economic, psychological and political explanations fit the political one best, backed by interviews. If forecasts are deliberately cooked, the outside view will be resisted.
numbers: Urban rail: average cost overrun about 45%, patronage about 50% lower than forecast, stable over the 70-year period.
limits: Kahneman and Lovallo replied that learning from other people's mistakes is not guaranteed (as quoted in Flyvbjerg 2022). Not settled. Both mechanisms can co-exist.
agent_relevance: For an agent there is no political incentive, so the cognitive cure should work on it. But if the prompt or user wants a rosy answer, the pull is similar, so the gate must be code-enforced.

source: Flyvbjerg, Budzier, Christodoulou and Zottoli (2024) Uniqueness bias: why it matters, how to curb it (Oxford working paper)
finding: Thinking a project is unique blocks the outside view and goes with worse outcomes. Managers rated how unique their IT projects were on a 1-10 scale; higher uniqueness went with larger cost overruns and a higher chance of extreme overruns.
numbers: N=219 IT projects (response rate 43-64%). Each extra point of uniqueness: about +5 percentage points of cost overrun (robust regression, p=0.01, lower CI bound 0.011 on the coefficient). A '10' project: about +45 points. Extreme overrun (76% or more): 37% risk at 10 vs 1% at 1 (logistic, p<0.001). 19.2% of projects rated themselves highly unique. In the sample the extreme tail was 23 times the normal-distribution expectation.
limits: Correlation, not experiment. Uniqueness ratings were gathered after the fact, so hindsight could colour them. Working paper, not peer reviewed when written. Response bias possible.
agent_relevance: A rule: 'this is a special case' is a warning flag, not a reason to skip the class lookup. The S0 gate should treat claimed uniqueness as a risk signal.

source: Flyvbjerg (2022) Top ten behavioral biases in project management: an overview (Project Management Journal)
finding: Review that ties the outside view to uniqueness bias, the planning fallacy (writ large), anchoring and escalation. Says the outside view includes unknown unknowns, since anything that went wrong in the class is already in the data. Quotes Kahneman (2011): in competition with the inside view, the outside view does not stand a chance. Treats anchoring on the base rate as the cure for WYSIATI (what you see is all there is).
numbers: No new data. Names the original planning fallacy as coined by Kahneman and Tversky (1979a, p. 315) and extended by Buehler et al. (1994, 1997).
limits: Review by a single advocate; the pieces are cited, not tested here. The 'planning fallacy writ large' covers costs, schedules and benefits, wider than the original task-time meaning.
agent_relevance: Supports ordering: base rate first as the anchor, then adjust. The outside view anchors on a meaningful number rather than a random one.

source: Gigerenzer and Hoffrage (1995) How to improve Bayesian reasoning without instruction: frequency formats. Psychological Review 102(4):684-704
finding: Base-rate neglect is largely about format. The same Bayesian problem in natural-frequency format (e.g. 10 out of 1,000) gave much more Bayesian reasoning than the probability format. The authors argue the mind is tuned to counts from natural sampling, not to percentages.
numbers: Study 1: 60 students, 15 problems. Bayesian answers 46% (standard menu) and 50% (short menu) with frequencies vs 16% and 28% with probabilities. Study 2: 24 problems. 84% of answers had an identifiable algorithm. Mammography problem: base rate 1%, hit rate 80%, false alarm 9.6%, correct answer 7.8%; in Eddy-type studies physicians mostly said 70-80%.
limits: Even the best condition left about half of answers non-Bayesian. Later work (Sloman et al. 2003, in the BBS source) found smaller gains. Strict joint criterion of process and outcome used.
agent_relevance: When giving the agent base-rate material, state it as counts ('9 of 100 such projects') not percentages. Code can convert.

source: Barbey and Sloman (2007) Base-rate respect: from ecological rationality to dual processes. Behavioral and Brain Sciences 30:241-297 (with commentaries)
finding: Review of base-rate neglect with the nested-sets account: neglect shrinks when the problem shows the set structure (which group is inside which), not only when frequencies are used. Early studies found neglect: only about 5% (Eddy 1982), 18% (Casscells 1978) and 10% of physicians (Hammerton 1973) gave the Bayesian answer, and the modal answer was the test's hit rate.
numbers: Single-event probability format: 12% (Cosmides and Tooby 1996) to 20% Bayesian; natural frequencies: 72% (Cosmides and Tooby) but only 51% in a Sloman et al. 2003 replication, and 31% in a further replication (gain not significant). 48 physicians (Gigerenzer 1996): 10% Bayesian with probabilities, 46% with frequencies.
limits: Target article plus dozens of commentaries. Replication gains from frequency format are smaller than first reported. The nested-sets account is itself disputed in the commentaries.
agent_relevance: A failed-replication line: frequency format helps, but less than first reported, and structure (sets nested) matters. When an agent explains the class to itself, show the nesting.

source: Griffin, Koehler and Brenner (2007) Commentary on Barbey and Sloman. BBS 30:268
finding: Counter-view: base-rate use is a case-based judgment issue. People judge the strength of evidence for the case at hand, and class information is added only to the degree it is read as relevant to this case. In a learning study, participants estimated the base rates they had seen accurately, yet their probability judgments were largely unaffected by them.
numbers: Lawyer-engineer paradigm (Kahneman and Tversky 1973): descriptions drawn from 70 engineers and 30 lawyers or 30 and 70. Base-rate use rises with counting procedures (Gigerenzer et al. 1988). In the stock-market learning study base rates were estimated accurately but not used, and willingness to pay showed the same neglect.
limits: Short commentary. Details of the learning studies are in Brenner et al. 2005, 2006, which we did not open.
agent_relevance: Knowing the base rate is not the same as using it. The gate must make the class rate a required input to the final number, by code.

source: Koehler (1996) The base rate fallacy reconsidered (as cited in Barbey and Sloman 2007)
finding: Koehler's review is cited for the lawyer-engineer finding that people rely on how representative a description is and under-use the population base rate, and for the point that neglect is not inevitable. We saw only the citations, not the paper.
numbers: Not available from this source beyond citations.
limits: Secondary mention only. Paper itself not opened.
agent_relevance: Treat 'people ignore base rates' as too strong: use rises when the rate is salient, causal or counted.

source: Buehler, Griffin and Ross (1994) JPSP 67(3):366-381, and (1995) It's about time; figures from a Wikipedia summary
finding: Planning fallacy in the lab: students asked to predict thesis time under-predicted. Paper itself paywalled and not read. Figures are from a secondary page.
numbers: 37 psychology students: mean prediction 33.9 days, best case 27.4, worst case 48.6, actual 55.5 days; about 30% finished within their own prediction. 1995 study: 13% finished by their 50% date, 19% by their 75% date, 45% by their 99% date.
limits: Secondary source, not checked against the paper. Even the worst-case forecast (48.6) was below the actual mean (55.5).
agent_relevance: Even stated worst cases are too optimistic, so 'consider the worst case' is not a substitute for the class distribution.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han and Steinhardt (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with language models. arXiv 2402.18563
finding: Retrieval-augmented LM forecaster. Its prompt asks the model, at step 6 after building an initial forecast from reasons for and against, to check if it is over or under confident and to consider 'the base rate of the event'. No ablation of the base-rate step in the text we read. Out-of-the-box models were poor.
numbers: Test set from June 2023 on, binary questions from 5 platforms. Brier: random 0.250, human crowd 0.149, best zero-shot model GPT-4-1106-Preview 0.208. System about 0.179 vs crowd 0.149 in one Table 3 row (labels garbled in extraction); average of system and crowd 0.146, better than the crowd alone.
limits: No test of the outside-view step alone. A base-rate reminder is one of many prompt parts. The 0.179 figure is read from a garbled table row; check against the paper before quoting.
agent_relevance: In published LLM forecasting systems the base rate is a late prompt reminder, not a gate. Our S0 puts it first. That order is untested here.

source: Flyvbjerg, Hon and Fok (2016) Hong Kong RCF paper, section on benefits of RCF (quotes Kahneman 2011)
finding: Reported (not measured) benefits of RCF in practice: UK use for over 10 years, mandatory for large rail and road in Denmark, used in Sweden, Switzerland, Norway and others. Claims that projects after RCF show lower overruns and that some projects were cancelled. Evidence given is an official's remark and project manager feedback.
numbers: No controlled comparison. Quotes Kahneman (2011, p. 251) endorsing RCF as a way to improve forecasts.
limits: Anecdotal. No before-after or randomised test in this paper. Which projects got RCF is unknown.
agent_relevance: Important gap: RCF is widely adopted but this source gives no controlled test of its effect on outcomes. Our agent evidence should come from our own benchmark runs (G7).

source: Kahneman and Lovallo (1993) Timid choices and bold forecasts: a cognitive perspective on risk taking. Management Science 39(1):17-31
finding: Core argument for why the inside view fails. The scenario of flawless execution of the plan may be more probable than any single scenario for a specific failure, yet the sum of the many ways to go wrong can still be larger. Choosing the most plausible scenario therefore overstates success, and outcomes with no easy scenario are wrongly treated as impossible. The outside view avoids scenario thinking (Dawes 1988) and keeps forecasts in the right range.
numbers: Worked example: a plan finishing on time versus one taking four times longer; no probabilities given.
quote: it is a serious error to assume that the outcomes of the most likely scenarios are also the most likely
limits: Verbal argument, not a formal model. The authors add that probabilities are treated as facts about the world for the exposition (footnote 7).
agent_relevance: Do not let the model choose the 'most likely story'. Sum over failure modes via class data. This supports the schema rule that code, not the model's narrative, sets the number.
